How Maine property tax works

Property tax in Maine is a local matter: each municipality assesses, bills and collects, and the bill follows ownership on April 1. 36 M.R.S. §502 fixes taxpayers and taxable property as of that date, and the tax year runs April 1 to March 31.

Due dates and interest are local choices. Under §505 a municipality votes the date or dates payment is due, the date interest starts (which is also the delinquency date), and the interest rate. The rate cannot go above the prime rate plus 3 percentage points as set by the Treasurer of State, and the maximum is posted by January 20 each year. A town may offer an early-payment discount of up to 10%.

Neighboring towns can send bills with different due dates, rates and ratios for houses worth the same. Read your own town's bill rather than a statewide average. For scale, the 2025 statewide commitment was $3,650,756,363 on $284,892,094,527 of taxable valuation, and town certified ratios ran from 50% to 112%.

How to challenge your assessment

File a written abatement application with the assessors within 185 days of commitment. 36 M.R.S. §841 lets the assessors abate for illegality, error or irregularity on an application inside that window, or on their own within one year. From one year out to three years, the municipal officers may act, but they cannot abate to fix a valuation error.

Prepare before you file:

  • Get the property record card and hunt for plain errors, like a wrong build year or lot size.
  • State the amount you want abated and the reason. You carry the burden of proof, and disagreeing with the value is not enough.
  • Gather evidence: errors on the card, recent sales of comparable nearby homes and neighborhood sales data.
  • If the assessor mailed a request for property information under §706-A, answer it. Skipping it may forfeit your appeal.
  • Expect a decision within 60 days. If none arrives in that time, the request is deemed denied.

Taxes stay due on the normal dates while an abatement is pending. The assessment is presumed valid, and under 36 M.R.S. §848-A it holds up when it is accurate within reasonable limits, unless you prove a deviation of 10% or more.

Appeals after a denial

A taxpayer has 60 days after a denial to appeal in writing to the local Board of Assessment Review. Under Section 843, if the board issues no written decision within 60 days, the application is deemed denied unless the applicant agrees in writing to wait longer.

Appeal levelWho hears itDeadline or rule
Abatement applicationAssessors185 days from commitment
Board of Assessment ReviewLocal board60 days after notice or deemed denial
Superior CourtResidential property, Rule 80BDirect appeal from the board, within 30 days
State Board of Property Tax ReviewNonresidential property or $1,000,000 or more60 days from the board decision

Where a town has no local board, the first appeal goes to the county commissioners. Homes appeal straight from the board to Superior Court. If your property is valued at $500,000 or more, you must pay the greater of last year's taxes (up to the current amount) or the undisputed current taxes while the appeal runs, or the appeal is suspended.

Falling behind: tax lien mortgages

Maine has no tax sale. It uses a tax lien mortgage instead. Between 8 months and one year after commitment, the collector may send a demand notice that gives 30 days to pay. If the bill stays open, a tax lien certificate is recorded at the registry of deeds within 10 days after that period ends (36 M.R.S. §942).

The recorded certificate becomes a tax lien mortgage under §943, and it ranks ahead of other liens. When the debt is still unpaid 18 months after recording, the mortgage is deemed foreclosed and the right to redeem ends. The treasurer must notify the owner and any mortgage holders 30 to 45 days before the foreclosure date.

  • Owners claiming the homestead exemption must be told about the hardship abatement process and where to get foreclosure-avoidance help.
  • The taxpayer pays recording and discharge fees, plus $13 and any foreclosure notice charge.
  • When an owner dies with a probated will, a probate judge may allow up to 60 more days to redeem.
  • After foreclosure the town holds title and can sell the property.

The 18-month clock is what matters. A sale that closes before it runs out pays the town from the proceeds and ends the problem.

Hardship relief and tax deferral

Under §841(2), municipal officers can abate taxes on a primary residence for a person who cannot pay because of hardship, within three years of commitment. They must give a written decision within 30 days of the application, and the proceedings are confidential.

Maine also runs a State Property Tax Deferral Program. You qualify if you are 65 or older, or unable to work because of a permanent disability, and you own a primary residence, have household income under $80,000, and hold liquid assets under $100,000 ($150,000 with more than one owner). The state pays the town and places a lien on the home. A sale of the home triggers repayment of the deferred taxes, interest and costs, and a new municipal lien blocks future deferral.

The Maine homestead exemption reduces taxable value by up to $25,000 for a permanent resident, adjusted by the local certified ratio.

Property tax at a Maine closing

A purchase contract can divide the year's tax by days of ownership. 36 M.R.S. §558 prorates taxes across the municipality's fiscal year unless the parties choose another period.

The town still bills whoever held title on April 1. When a sale changes the owner, §502 lets the assessor update the records after a declaration of value is filed, and the tax notice goes to both the new owner and the April 1 owner of record.

Transfer tax is a separate charge. The state collects $2.20 per $500 of value, shared evenly by buyer and seller under §4641-A. Value above $1,000,000 adds $3.80 per $500 on the excess.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Maine houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

  1. Phone the town tax collector and ask for a payoff that includes interest and any lien charges.
  2. Search the registry of deeds for a lien certificate. If one is recorded, count months from its date.
  3. Pull the assessor's record card and compare it against what the house really is.
  4. Note the abatement dates. The 185 days begin at commitment, roughly when bills first go out.
  5. Disclose any deferral lien to buyers, since the state is repaid when title transfers.

A house with back taxes, a lien and deferred repairs is a hard sell on the open market. A cash sale avoids the buyer's lender, and the payoff is paid from proceeds at closing. Cash Home Buyers purchases Maine houses in any condition, and we name a price only after seeing the property.

Frequently asked questions

When is Maine property tax assessed?

On April 1. Whoever owns the property that day is taxed for the year ahead.

How long do I have to apply for an abatement?

185 days from commitment. After that, officials may still act on their own initiative for a limited time.

Can I appeal if the assessor says no?

Yes, in writing to the local Board of Assessment Review, within 60 days of the denial or deemed denial. A homeowner who loses there can go to Superior Court under Rule 80B.

Does Maine hold tax sales?

No. Maine uses a tax lien mortgage. If it stays unpaid 18 months after the certificate is recorded, the mortgage is deemed foreclosed and redemption ends.

What happens to a deferred tax balance when I sell?

The state is repaid the full deferred amount, with interest and costs, when you sell or transfer.

title: Maine Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home
content:
Maine Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home

Cash Home Buyers in Maine
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Maine Homestead Exemption: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Maine Homestead Exemption sale
  • Turn the Maine Homestead Exemption offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Maine House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Maine?
We buy Maine houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

What the Maine homestead exemption takes off

The Maine homestead exemption lowers the taxable value of your permanent home by up to $25,000. The amount is adjusted by your town's certified ratio, so a town with an 80% ratio gives an exemption of $20,000. It cannot exceed the value of the homestead itself.

Under 36 M.R.S. §683 the $25,000 has two pieces: $10,000 of just value in the base subsection, plus an additional $15,000 for tax years that began on or after April 1, 2020. It sits on top of other exemptions a homeowner may already hold, such as those in sections 653 and 654-A. It is not a credit on the bill. It shrinks the value the town multiplies by its tax rate.

The exemption is tied to a person who lives in the house, not to the house itself. When ownership or residence changes, the break stops and the next owner has to qualify separately.

Who qualifies

You qualify if you are a permanent Maine resident, the home is your permanent residence, and you have owned a home in Maine for the twelve months before you apply.

  • Camps, vacation homes and second residences do not count. You can have only one permanent residence at a time.
  • The home must be residential property assessed as real property. A mobile home on a rented lot may qualify.
  • Permanent residence is presumed to continue until circumstances show otherwise. The test is whether you intend to return when you are away.
  • There is no income limit, but renters do not qualify.
  • With several owners, one signature is enough on the application. The exemption can be divided among co-owners who live there in proportion to their interests.

A person who loses a homestead to tax lien foreclosure and later gets it back from the municipality is treated as having owned it the whole time. The town's brief ownership does not disqualify them.

How and when to file

File a written application with your municipal assessor on or before April 1. A form filed after April 1 applies to the next year's assessment, so a late application costs a full tax year of savings.

Most towns hand out the form, and Maine Revenue Services posts it on its property tax forms page. For an owner-occupied house the town where the property sits and the town where you live are the same, so call the assessor if yours is not.

You do not need to renew every year. The exemption stays in place as long as ownership and residency stay the same. If an assessor denies the application, the notice must give reasons, and you can appeal in writing to the local Board of Assessment Review or the county commissioners. Denials of homestead, veteran and blind exemptions can also go through the abatement process.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Maine house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What changes on April 1, 2027

The old section 683 discontinues its exemptions for property tax years beginning on or after April 1, 2027, and a new section, 36 M.R.S. §683-A, takes over from that date. The base homestead exemption stays at $25,000 of just value, and veteran and blind exemptions move into the same statute.

ExemptionAmount from April 1, 2027
Base homestead exemption (§683-A)Up to $25,000 of just value
Veteran, age 62 or olderUp to $6,000
Veteran with 100% service-connected ratingUp to $50,000
Legally blind permanent residentUp to $5,000

Current holders do not reapply unless they qualify for a higher amount. Applications for the higher amounts go to the local assessor before April 1, 2027, and the figures are multiplied by the local certified ratio. Both statutes tie the exemption to a permanent resident who has owned the homestead for the preceding 12 months.

Selling a house with a homestead exemption

The exemption affects who owes what in the year of the sale, and it can change what a buyer pays the next year. Maine taxes what you own on April 1, and the tax year runs April 1 to March 31 under 36 M.R.S. §502.

Closing usually involves a proration. Under §558 a buyer and seller may split property tax pro rata over the municipality's fiscal year, unless they agree on a different period. Your bill already reflects your exemption for that year, so the proration uses the lower number.

A buyer does not inherit your exemption. A buyer who will live in the house files their own application by April 1, and the town applies it to the next assessment. A buyer who cannot meet the twelve-month ownership test, or who plans to rent the house out, may not get the same bill you did. Tell a buyer who is looking only at your old tax bill.

The state also charges a real estate transfer tax of $2.20 per $500 of value, split equally between buyer and seller under §4641-A.

Inheriting a house that had a homestead exemption

An inherited house that no one lives in will usually lose the exemption, because it rests on the owner using the home as a permanent residence. The break stays in effect only while ownership and residency are unchanged. Ask the assessor how the town handles a death.

Heirs who plan to sell should watch the April 1 date. If the owner died after April 1 and the exemption was in place that day, the town has already set that year's bill. If the house sits vacant into the next tax year, expect a full bill with no exemption. Our Maine probate guide explains who has authority to sell the property.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Maine houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

The state tax deferral program

The State Property Tax Deferral Program matters most at closing. To qualify, you must be 65 or older or unable to work due to permanent disability, with household income under $80,000 and liquid assets under $100,000 ($150,000 with multiple owners). The state pays the tax, then places a lien on the home. Selling or transferring the home requires repayment of all deferred taxes, interest and costs. If a sale ends your time in the program, the payoff comes out of your proceeds.

Check your homestead status before listing

  • Owners who moved out and are renting the house. The home is no longer the permanent residence, so the exemption may have ended.
  • Owners who bought a second Maine home in the last year. You can have only one permanent residence.
  • Heirs holding a vacant house. Ownership has changed and residence has stopped.
  • Owners with a deferral lien. Expect a payoff figure from Maine Revenue Services at closing.

If any of these fits and the house needs work you cannot afford before a sale, a direct sale to a cash buyer can simplify the tax side, since there is no buyer financing or inspection renegotiation holding up the proration. That is the kind of situation Cash Home Buyers works with, and we do not promise a price until we see the property.

Frequently asked questions

Is the Maine homestead exemption still $25,000?

Yes. It is up to $25,000 of just value, multiplied by your town's certified ratio, and the base stays at $25,000 under the new section starting April 1, 2027.

What is the deadline to apply, and do I reapply every year?

April 1, filed with your municipal assessor. A form filed after April 1 applies to the next year's assessment. You do not reapply each year, since the exemption stays in effect while ownership and residency do not change.

Does the buyer get my homestead exemption when I sell?

No. The exemption belongs to the permanent resident who owns and lives in the home. A buyer who will live there files their own application by April 1.

Can I get the exemption on a camp or second home?

No. Camps, vacation homes and second residences do not qualify, and you can have only one permanent residence at a time.

Will the exemption stop in 2027?

The old section 683 is discontinued for tax years beginning April 1, 2027, but section 683-A takes over with a base exemption of up to $25,000, plus veteran and blind exemptions.

title: Maine Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling
content:
Maine Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

Cash Home Buyers in Maine
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Maine Estate and Inheritance Tax sale
  • Turn the Maine Estate and Inheritance Tax offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Maine House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Maine?
We buy Maine houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Maine estate tax or inheritance tax?

Maine has an estate tax and no inheritance tax. The tax is figured on the whole estate before it is distributed, so heirs do not owe a separate tax on what they receive. The estate tax fully replaced the old inheritance tax for deaths after June 30, 1986.

For a family holding a house, the practical questions are whether the estate is large enough to owe anything, and whether the paperwork for the lien release is in order. Some estates owe no tax and still file a short form so the house can be sold with a clean title. Bring the date of death, the house's deed reference and a value for the property to the first conversation with the estate's attorney, since those three items drive every form below.

Definitions are in 36 M.R.S. §4102. The "adjusted federal gross estate" is the federal gross estate adjusted for Maine elective property, plus taxable gifts made in the year before death. A "resident" is a person domiciled in Maine at death, and a "nonresident" is someone domiciled elsewhere.

The 2026 exclusion amount

For 2026 deaths, Maine's exclusion amount is $7,160,000. It was $7,000,000 for 2025, $6,800,000 for 2024 and $6,410,000 for 2023, so it creeps up from year to year. The federal exclusion for 2026 decedents is $15,000,000, as set out in the Form 706ME instructions. The gap between the two is why a Maine estate can owe state tax when no federal return is needed.

Estate tax rates

Tax applies only to the amount above the exclusion, in three steps. Table A in the 2026 Form 706ME instructions sets the rates.

Maine taxable amount (line 5)Tax
$7,160,000 or less$0
Over $7,160,000 up to $10,160,0008% of the amount over $7,160,000
Over $10,160,000 up to $13,160,000$240,000 plus 10% of the amount over $10,160,000
Over $13,160,000$540,000 plus 12% of the amount over $13,160,000

Interest and penalties are added to the tax owed. They cannot be deducted on the return.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Maine house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Who must file a Maine estate tax return

A Maine return is required when the estate is above the threshold or when a federal estate tax return is required. Any one of these triggers it:

  • A federal estate tax return is required.
  • The federal gross estate plus taxable gifts made within one year of death plus Maine elective property exceeds the threshold.
  • The Maine QTIP election on line 2 of Form 706ME is greater than zero.

Form 706ME applies to Maine residents, and to nonresidents who owned Maine real or tangible personal property at death. A nonresident who held Maine land through a trust, LLC or other pass-through entity may still be treated as owning Maine property, unless the entity had a valid business purpose, carried on a for-profit business and was acquired in a bona fide sale for full consideration. The personal representative files. If none has been appointed, a person in possession of the estate's property is treated as the representative.

Due dates and extensions

The return is due nine months after the date of death. Maine gives an automatic extension to file equal to any federal extension or six months, whichever is longer.

  • An extension to file does not extend the time to pay. Tax is due by the original date, and interest runs on unpaid tax.
  • A longer extension must be requested in writing before the automatic six-month period ends, and the total generally cannot exceed eight months.
  • Estates largely made up of closely held business interests may request a payment extension under 36 M.R.S. §4109.
  • Penalties may be waived for reasonable cause. Interest waivers are rare.

Form 706ME must be filed and paid electronically through the Maine Tax Portal, which needs no account for estate tax filings.

The estate tax lien and your house sale

Maine law puts an automatic lien on a decedent's Maine real and tangible personal property at death (36 M.R.S. §4112). A buyer's title company will want a release before it insures the purchase, so the lien matters whenever an estate sells a house.

The representative requests the release with a Certificate of Discharge of Estate Tax Lien, plus either Form 706ME or Form 700-SOV (Statement of Value) and any required proof of value. The State Tax Assessor signs the certificate and mails it back, and the original is recorded with the county Registry of Deeds.

  • When no return is otherwise required, the estate files Form 700-SOV with the certificate to request the release.
  • Probate courts may require Form 700-SOV or 706ME even when no tax is owed.
  • If you lack the deed's book and page, the Registry of Deeds can help you find the reference.

Maine has 17 registry of deeds offices, one for each county and two for Aroostook, so send the certificate to the office where the house sits.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Maine houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Timing an estate sale around the lien

Start the paperwork early. The release is often what sets the closing date, and even a small estate with one house benefits from a clear timeline.

  1. Confirm the date of death and the value of all assets to see whether the estate is near the $7,160,000 threshold.
  2. Get a date-of-death appraisal of the house. The same value is generally used for the heirs' basis under IRS Publication 551.
  3. Prepare Form 700-SOV or Form 706ME with the Certificate of Discharge.
  4. Submit electronically through the Maine Tax Portal and wait for the signed certificate.
  5. Record the original at the registry of deeds in the county where the house is located.
  6. Schedule the closing after the release is recorded.

Probate steps run alongside this, as described in our Maine probate guide. A personal representative needs authority from the probate court to sign a deed, so line up those letters at the same time.

Selling an estate house for cash

A cash buyer can close without bank underwriting, but the lien release and the estate's authority still set the timeline. Heirs often come to us with a house that needs repairs, or one that sits empty while the family decides what to do. We buy as-is and work with your attorney or personal representative on the documents the title company needs.

For a specific estate, check with the personal representative's attorney or Maine Revenue Services before you sign a purchase contract.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Maine estate tax threshold in 2026?

$7,160,000. Estates below that generally owe no Maine estate tax, though a form may still be needed to release the lien on real estate. The amount was $7,000,000 for 2025 and $6,800,000 for 2024.

Does Maine have an inheritance tax?

No. Maine uses an estate tax only, figured on the estate rather than on each heir's share. It fully replaced the old inheritance tax for deaths after June 30, 1986.

Can heirs sell an inherited house in Maine before the estate tax is paid?

Usually the title company will require the Certificate of Discharge of Estate Tax Lien first. The lien attaches automatically at death, and the release is recorded at the county registry of deeds. Ask the personal representative's attorney how to time it.

What is Form 700-SOV?

It is the Statement of Value, which an estate files with a certificate request to release the lien when no estate tax return is otherwise required. Probate courts may ask for it even when no tax is owed.

When is the Maine estate tax return due?

Nine months after the date of death. Maine allows an automatic filing extension of six months or the federal extension, whichever is longer, but payment is still due by the original date.

Selling a Maine House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Maine houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

How a Maine eviction works

A Maine landlord must serve a written notice, file a court case, win a judgment, and then wait for a writ of possession that a sheriff or constable serves. The court case is called a forcible entry and detainer action, or FED, and 14 M.R.S. Chapter 709 governs it.

Every step has strict paperwork, and a defective notice or a missed service step can reset the clock. If you own a rented house and may sell, find out where the case stands, because the stage it has reached decides what a buyer can do. This is general information, not legal advice.

Which notice comes first?

It depends on why the tenancy is ending. For a tenancy at will, 14 M.R.S. §6002 lets either side end it with at least 30 days' written notice, or with a 7-day notice for specific grounds.

NoticeWhen it is usedRequirements
30-day noticeEnding a tenancy at will without a stated faultMust tell the tenant of the right to contest in court; if rent is paid past the 30 days, the notice must expire on or after that date
7-day noticeRent 7 or more days in arrears, nuisance, substantial damage not repaired, unauthorized occupant, and certain violence-related groundsMust state the specific ground; a rent notice must state the amount owed and the cure statement

A landlord can combine a 30-day and a 7-day notice in one document. A clerical error in the arrears figure does not void the notice if it was unintentional and does not materially change its purpose. Landlords must also attach the judicial branch's form notice to termination notices under 14 M.R.S. §6001.

How a tenant can stop an eviction for unpaid rent

By paying. If the tenant pays the full rent due before a 7-day arrears notice expires, the notice is void. After it expires, paying all arrears, rent due and the filing and service fees before the writ issues reinstates the tenancy, and no writ may issue.

Payment, or written assurance of payment, through the general assistance program counts as cash here. For a landlord planning a sale, that means a nonpayment case can end suddenly when rent arrives.

A tenant can also raise the implied warranty of habitability in a nonpayment case. The landlord must have had actual or constructive notice of the problem and unreasonably failed to make repairs, and the tenant must not have caused it. If the court finds the unit unfit, the tenant owes only reduced fair rental value until repairs are made. The duty itself sits in 14 M.R.S. §6021, which also covers heat and mold.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Maine house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Court steps and costs for a rent case

Maine courts lay out a seven-step path for evicting a tenant who has not paid rent.

  1. Serve a 7-day notice to quit under §6002(1), with the information sheet (form CV-256).
  2. Prepare the complaint (CV-007), summons (CV-034, $5 each from the clerk) and the other required forms. List all tenants and add "and all other occupants" if others live there.
  3. Serve the papers through the county sheriff only after the notice period ends.
  4. File the notice to quit, the complaint, the summons with the return of service and the lease, with a $100 filing fee, before the hearing.
  5. Attend the hearing even if the tenant does not. Mediation is available at the court that day at no extra cost.
  6. If you win, you receive a judgment for possession and a writ of possession.
  7. If the tenant has not left, buy the writ from the clerk and hire a sheriff to serve it.

An eviction does not collect back rent. That takes a separate case, often in Small Claims Court. If a tenant cannot be served in hand after three good-faith attempts on three different days, 14 M.R.S. §6004 permits first-class mail plus leaving a copy at the tenant's last and usual residence, with an affidavit filed.

Time to leave after judgment

The court issues the writ of possession seven calendar days after judgment is entered. Once a sheriff or constable serves it, the tenant has 48 hours to leave under 14 M.R.S. §6005.

A tenant who stays past 48 hours is treated as a trespasser, and the belongings are considered abandoned under §6013. No writ issues if the tenancy ended for rent arrears and the tenant paid the amount needed to reinstate.

An appeal can slow things down. Under §6008, either party may appeal to Superior Court, and a defendant who appeals must pay the lesser of the unpaid current month's rent or the arrearage. The court can stay the writ on conditions such as continued rent payments. The deadline is the earlier of the writ's issuance or 30 days after judgment.

A tenant's belongings after eviction

The landlord must store them in a safe, dry, secured location and send written notice by first-class mail with proof of mailing. 14 M.R.S. §6013 sets the timing.

  • The notice must include an itemized list of the items and containers.
  • The tenant has 7 days from the notice to claim the property.
  • If the tenant responds, the landlord must keep storing it for at least 14 days after sending the notice.
  • A tenant who claims the property within 7 days cannot be charged fees or other amounts as a condition of release.
  • Unclaimed property may be sold at a reasonable fair market price. Proceeds go first to back rent, damages and costs, and any balance goes to the Treasurer of State.
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Maine houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What can stop or delay an eviction

The statute builds in several defenses. Section 6001 presumes retaliation, subject to rebuttal, if within 6 months before the action the tenant asserted listed statutory rights, complained in good faith about code violations, made written repair requests or filed fair housing complaints. A writ cannot issue without rebuttal.

  • A tenant may raise a landlord's failure to provide a reasonable accommodation for a disability.
  • Victims of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking cannot be evicted for those incidents.
  • A bona fide tenancy in a building with a pending foreclosure may be ended only under the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act of 2009.
  • A new owner or assignee generally cannot bring the process against a tenant at will unless that tenant received proper notice under §6002.

When the owner sells a Maine rental

Security deposits must be accounted for and transferred no later than the real estate closing. Under 14 M.R.S. §6035, whoever holds the deposits, whether landlord, agent or executor, must either transfer them to the successor with an accounting or return them to the tenants.

  • The seller mails each tenant notice of the transfer, the new owner's name and address, and a copy of the accounting.
  • At closing, the seller gives the buyer written proof of the accounting and transfer.
  • Once the holder complies, it is relieved of further liability for those funds, and the buyer takes on the landlord's duties.
  • Under §6038, deposits must sit in a bank account protected from the landlord's creditors, and a tenant can recover the greater of actual damages, $500 or one month's rent for a violation.

A tenant with a lease generally stays through a sale, because the buyer steps into the landlord's place. A buyer who wants the house empty must wait for the lease to end or follow the notice rules above.

Evict first or sell with tenants in place?

It comes down to timing and cost. An eviction can take weeks, adds filing and sheriff fees, and ends with a unit that may need work. Selling with tenants avoids that, but the buyer must accept the lease and the deposit transfer.

We buy Maine houses with tenants, unpaid rent or deferred repairs, as-is. A cash sale lets you hand off the property without waiting for a court date. If you are in the middle of a case, talk to a Maine attorney before you sign anything, and make sure the closing includes the deposit accounting that §6035 requires.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

How long does a Maine eviction take?

It depends on the notice period, the hearing date and whether the tenant appeals. The fixed pieces are a 7-day or 30-day notice, a writ issued 7 calendar days after judgment, and 48 hours for the tenant to leave once the writ is served.

How much notice does a Maine landlord have to give?

At least 30 days' written notice to end a tenancy at will, or a 7-day notice for grounds such as rent 7 or more days late, nuisance or substantial damage. A lease may add its own terms.

What is the filing fee for an eviction in Maine?

A rent case carries a $100 filing fee, plus $5 for each summons from the clerk. Writ and sheriff service fees are separate.

Can I sell a house in Maine while the tenant is still there?

Yes. The tenant's lease generally continues with the new owner. At closing the seller must transfer or return security deposits, give the buyer written proof, and mail each tenant notice of the transfer.

What if the tenant pays after getting a 7-day notice?

Paying all rent due before the notice expires voids it. Paying all arrears and filing and service fees after expiration but before the writ issues reinstates the tenancy, and no writ may issue.

content:
Maine Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Cash Home Buyers in Maine
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Maine Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property sale
  • Turn the Maine Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Maine House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Maine?
We buy Maine houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

How Maine probate works

Each of Maine's 16 counties has its own probate court, and that court runs the process. Courts there handle the estates of deceased and missing persons, plus guardianships, trusts, name changes and adoptions. Start in the county of the decedent's last home.

The governing law is the Maine Probate Code, Title 18-C of the Maine Revised Statutes. Most estates begin with an application to the register of probate. The register can issue a written statement of informal probate under 18-C M.R.S. §3-302, but only after 120 hours have gone by since the death. It remains in force until a formal testacy proceeding replaces it.

Forms can be filed electronically. The e-filing fee is $7, and court fees, surcharges, newspaper publication and certified mail can add to the total. Clerks cannot advise you on the law, which is why families often hire a lawyer for anything beyond a plain estate.

Who can be personal representative?

Priority starts with whoever the will names, then moves down through the spouse, devisees, heirs and last of all creditors. The full ranking is in Section 3-203. Anyone 18 or older whom a court has not found unsuitable in a formal proceeding can serve.

  • The will's own choice, including a person nominated under a power the will grants, ranks first.
  • A spouse who also inherits under the will ranks next, followed by other devisees, then a spouse with no devise, then other heirs.
  • A creditor may ask to be appointed once forty-five days have gone by since death. If nothing has been opened six months after death, the State Tax Assessor may apply.
  • Anyone entitled to letters can nominate another person, and anyone can step aside with a written renunciation filed in court.

Objecting to an appointment requires a formal proceeding. When heirs fight over who should serve, the house usually sits until it is settled.

Selling the house without a judge's approval

Usually the representative can sell and never needs to ask a judge. Under §3-711, the representative gets the powers an absolute owner has over title, held in trust for creditors and other interested people, and can use them with no hearing or order unless the section says otherwise.

The biggest limit is a waiting period for heirs. Before any sale or transfer of an interest in estate real property, the representative must give those heirs notice at least 10 days ahead, unless the will lets the sale go forward without notice. Section 3-715 adds authority to mortgage or lease estate property, or to sell it privately or at auction on cash or credit terms, subject to anything the will or a formal court order provides.

A cash sale follows three steps: sign the purchase agreement, send the 10-day heir notice, then sign the deed at closing as personal representative. Read the will before you start, since a will can narrow or widen these powers.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Maine house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

The small estate affidavit and real estate

Maine offers an affidavit for collecting personal property, and personal property is all it covers. Section 3-1201 lets a successor use it when three things are true: the estate's total value after liens and encumbrances is no higher than $40,000 as adjusted for inflation, a month has run since the death, and nobody has a petition pending to appoint a personal representative.

Since the 2025 amendment, each county probate court posts the current inflation-adjusted figure on its website every year. The affidavit reaches debts owed to the dead person and property held by others. Title to a house is outside its reach, so an estate with a house needs a personal representative appointed the ordinary way.

Creditor deadlines and probate time limits

Claims are generally cut off nine months after death, or sooner if the notice period ends first. Under Section 3-803, a claim that arose before death is barred unless it is presented by the earlier of those two dates.

StepTime limit
Informal probate by the registerAt least 120 hours after death
Small estate affidavitA month after death, with the estate under $40,000 (inflation adjusted)
Notice to creditors by publicationTwo weekly notices, claims due 4 months after the first
Mailed notice to a known creditorThe later of 4 months from publication and 60 days from mailing
Claims arising before deathEarlier of 9 months or the notice period
Last date to open probateThree years from death, with exceptions

The notice is published weekly, twice, in a general-circulation newspaper serving the decedent's county. A mortgage or other lien survives the claims bar. The State can still pursue Medicaid reimbursement if it files within four months of notice.

How long can heirs wait to open probate?

Probate generally cannot be opened after three years from the date of death. Section 3-108 sets that limit and lists exceptions. One exception permits a late proceeding to confirm title when the first three years passed with no activity. In that case the representative's authority is limited, and only administration expenses can be claimed against the estate.

A contest of an informally probated will can be filed until the later of 12 months from informal probate or three years from death. Waiting that long narrows what a representative can do with the house, so heirs who plan to sell usually move well before the deadline.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Maine houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Transfer tax, property tax and fees

An estate that sells owes the state transfer tax; an estate that distributes to an heir does not. The rate in 36 M.R.S. §4641-A is $2.20 for every $500 of value, and the buyer and seller each owe half. Section 4641-C carves out deeds of distribution under Title 18-C, parent-to-child deeds with no payment, and transfer-on-death deeds.

A deed of distribution hands the house to an heir. A deed from the representative to a stranger who pays for the house is a sale. The exemption list is silent on a representative who sells to a buyer, so ask the registry of deeds or an attorney how the deed should be drafted.

Property tax is fixed by who owned the property on April 1 (36 M.R.S. §502), so the estate owes that year's bill. Buyer and seller can then prorate across the town's fiscal year under §558. Our Maine property tax guide covers abatements and tax liens, and the homestead exemption page explains how a vacant inherited house can lose the exemption.

Problems heirs run into with inherited houses

  • Heirs split over the choice of representative or over selling at all. Any objection to an appointment has to be brought as a formal proceeding.
  • The house has unpaid property tax. Maine uses tax lien mortgages. Where the owner left a probated will, a probate judge can grant up to 60 extra days to redeem once the will is allowed or disallowed (36 M.R.S. §943).
  • Nobody lives there and repairs slide. A representative may hold assets until distribution and may pay for repairs, but spending estate cash calls for a plan.
  • Heirs live out of state. Electronic filing helps, and a representative can sell without every heir present once the 10-day notice has gone out.

If the estate's house needs work, a cash buyer lets the representative skip repairs and staging and sell as-is. Cash Home Buyers makes offers on Maine estate properties, and accepting is the representative's call. Any figure comes only after we see the house.

A workable order: find the will and file it, get letters issued, order death certificates and ask the town for a tax payoff. Then send the 10-day heir notice before anyone signs a purchase agreement.

Frequently asked questions

Can a Maine estate avoid probate?

Sometimes it can skip it. The §3-1201 affidavit covers estates of $40,000 or less (inflation adjusted), yet it only collects personal property. For a house, plan on a personal representative.

Which court hears Maine probate?

The probate court of the county where the decedent lived. You can e-file, and each of the 16 counties runs its own court.

Does a Maine representative need a judge's approval to sell?

Usually not. Section 3-711 gives the representative an owner's power over title, with one catch: heirs get at least 10 days' notice before the sale unless the will waives it.

How long do creditors have to file claims?

Nine months from death, or less if the notice period ends first. A published notice gives creditors 4 months from the first printing.

Is transfer tax due on an estate house sale?

Yes on a sale: $2.20 per $500 of value, shared by buyer and seller. A Title 18-C deed of distribution to an heir is exempt.

Maine Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Cash Home Buyers in Maine
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Maine Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Maine Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House sale
  • Turn the Maine Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Maine House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Maine?
We buy Maine houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Maine tax capital gains on a house sale?

No Maine rate is set aside for capital gains on homes. Under 36 M.R.S. §5121, a resident's Maine taxable income starts with federal adjusted gross income, so any taxable profit from your house lands on the Maine return and is taxed at the ordinary graduated rates.

Your bill turns on two things: how much profit the federal exclusion removes, and where the remainder falls on the Maine schedule for your filing status.

The answers depend on facts the sale price alone cannot show: how long you lived in the house, what you paid for it, what you spent on improvements, and whether you live in Maine now. Work through each piece below to estimate the bill before you sign anything.

The federal home sale exclusion

A homeowner who lived in the property can usually shelter $250,000 of profit from tax, or $500,000 when filing jointly (IRS Topic 701). Sheltered profit is left out of federal adjusted gross income, which means Maine never sees it.

  • Ownership: you or your spouse held title for at least 24 months of the 5 years ending on the sale date.
  • Use: you and your spouse each lived there as a main home for at least 24 months of those same 5 years.
  • Frequency: generally off the table if you excluded gain on a different home sale in the 2 years before this one.
  • Reporting: a Form 1099-S has to be reported even when every dollar of gain is excludable. Any gain that is not excludable goes on Form 8949 and Schedule D.

The two years of ownership and the two years of use need not overlap, provided both fit inside the five-year window. IRS Publication 523 covers partial exclusions and depreciation.

Maine income tax rates on gain you cannot exclude

For 2026 Maine uses three brackets: 5.8 percent, 6.75 percent and 7.15 percent. The thresholds are in the 2026 Maine Revenue Services rate schedule.

Filing status5.8% applies below6.75% bracket7.15% applies at or above
Single or married filing separately$27,400$27,400 to $64,850$64,850
Head of household$41,100$41,100 to $97,300$97,300
Married filing jointly$54,850$54,850 to $129,750$129,750

Starting with tax years beginning in 2026, a 2 percent surcharge applies to Maine taxable income above $1,000,000 for a single filer, $750,000 for married filing separately, and $1,500,000 for married filing jointly or head of household. A large gain from a high-value house or a multi-parcel sale can reach that level.

The 2026 standard deduction is $15,700 for a single filer and $31,400 for a joint return, plus a $5,300 personal exemption per taxpayer.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Maine house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

The federal rate on a taxable gain

Once you have held a house longer than a year, the profit is long-term and the federal rate is 0, 15 or 20 percent depending on income (IRS Topic 409 explains the holding period).

  • For taxable years beginning in 2025, the 0 percent rate applies at or below $48,350 (single), $96,700 (married filing jointly) or $64,750 (head of household).
  • The 15 percent rate covers income up to $533,400 (single), $600,050 (married filing jointly) or $566,700 (head of household).
  • Above those amounts the rate is 20 percent.
  • A house sold after one year or less produces short-term gain, taxed as ordinary income.
  • Unrecaptured section 1250 gain, a slice of the profit tied to depreciation, is taxed at 25 percent at most.

Maine tax comes on top of the federal bill and follows the Maine brackets above, whichever federal rate you land in.

Selling a Maine house from out of state

A nonresident who sells for $100,000 or more has 2.5 percent of the price held back at closing by the buyer or closing agent. Individuals, estates and businesses all fall under the rule (Maine Revenue Services real estate withholding FAQ).

  • The amount held back is an estimated payment toward Maine tax on the gain, not the final bill.
  • When there are several owners, the buyer takes 2.5 percent of each nonresident seller's share.
  • Form REW-1 and the payment are due from the buyer or escrow person within 30 days of closing.
  • A Maine resident who does not hand over a signed residency affidavit (Form REW-2 or REW-3) is treated as a nonresident for this purpose.
  • A partnership counts as a Maine resident if at least 75 percent of its ownership is held by Maine residents on the transfer date.

Heirs who live elsewhere are often caught off guard. An estate that sells Maine property is covered too, so expect the closing agent to ask for a residency affidavit or an exemption certificate.

Reducing or avoiding the 2.5 percent withholding

Send Form REW-5 to Maine Revenue Services before closing. Nothing can be granted afterward, and the office wants at least 5 business days to respond.

  • Full exemption: possible when there is no gain, or when the federal principal residence exclusion applies. Ask for it on REW-5.
  • Reduction: possible when your maximum Maine tax on the gain falls below 2.5 percent of the price. The maximum is 7.15 percent of the gain, plus 2 percent of the gain above $1,000,000 (single), $1,500,000 (head of household or married filing jointly) or $750,000 (married filing separately) for tax year 2026.
  • Estates and trusts use 7.15 percent plus 2 percent of gain above $1,000,000. Corporations use 8.93 percent.
  • A like-kind exchange under IRC §1031 still triggers withholding, but you can request an exemption with REW-5 and a copy of the exchange contract.
  • Installment sales may qualify for a reduction based on first-year gain.

Selling under $100,000 avoids withholding, yet a federally taxable gain is taxable in Maine at any amount. To get back excess withholding, a nonresident files a Maine income tax return for the sale year. Refund claims are generally due within three years of the return due date or three years from payment, whichever is later.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Maine houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How an inherited house changes the numbers

Heirs generally start from what the house was worth when the owner died rather than what the owner paid. IRS Publication 551 covers the options: fair market value at death, the alternate valuation date when the estate elects it, and special-use valuation for qualifying farm or business property.

An estate that filed a federal Form 706 usually sends beneficiaries a Schedule A (Form 8971), and some beneficiaries must adopt the reported value as basis. There is one carve-out: property you or your spouse gave to the decedent within a year of death carries the decedent's adjusted basis instead.

In practice, a Maine house sold a year or two after inheritance often shows little or no gain. Estate-side issues, including Maine's own estate tax lien, are covered in our Maine estate tax guide. Basis is generally what you paid, plus improvements that add value, minus allowable depreciation (IRS Topic 703).

A cash sale and Maine tax planning

Selling for cash leaves the tax rules as they are but fixes the closing date, so you know the tax year, the day the gain is realized and when any withholding falls due. A nonresident can file the REW-5 request early too.

People call us about inherited houses, tenant-occupied rentals and homes with deferred repairs. Each carries its own tax issue: basis for heirs, depreciation for landlords, withholding for owners who left the state. Run your own figures past a tax professional. We make a plain offer and leave the filings to your closing agent and accountant.

Frequently asked questions

Does Maine tax the profit when I sell my house?

Yes, if the gain is taxable. A resident's Maine income starts from federal adjusted gross income, so any gain not excluded under the federal home sale rules is taxed at Maine's graduated rates. For 2026 those rates are 5.8, 6.75 and 7.15 percent.

How much of my gain can I exclude when selling my Maine home?

Up to $250,000, or $500,000 on a joint return, if you owned and lived in the house as your main home for at least 24 months of the last 5 years. You generally cannot use it if you excluded gain on another home within the prior 2 years.

What is Maine real estate withholding?

It is a 2.5 percent withholding on the sale price when a nonresident sells Maine property for $100,000 or more. The buyer or closing agent files Form REW-1 and pays within 30 days of closing. It is only an estimate of the seller's Maine tax.

Can I get the withholding waived?

Possibly. File Form REW-5 with Maine Revenue Services before closing. Exemptions or reductions are available in cases such as no gain, a federal principal residence exclusion, or when your maximum Maine tax is below 2.5 percent of the price. It cannot be requested after closing.

Do heirs owe Maine tax on an inherited house they sell?

Only on gain above their basis. Inherited property generally takes its fair market value at the date of death as basis, so a sale soon after inheritance often shows little gain. A nonresident heir may still face withholding at closing.

title: Maine Real Estate Transfer Tax: Rates, Exemptions and Who Pays
content:
Maine Real Estate Transfer Tax: Rates, Exemptions and Who Pays

Cash Home Buyers in Maine
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Maine Real Estate Transfer Tax: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Maine Real Estate Transfer Tax sale
  • Turn the Maine Real Estate Transfer Tax offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Maine House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Maine?
We buy Maine houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Transfer tax rate

Maine charges $2.20 on each $500 of a property's value, counting any fraction of $500 as a full unit. For transfers on or after November 1, 2025, value above $1 million carries an added $3.80 per $500, which puts that top slice at $6.00 per $500. The rate is set in 36 M.R.S. section 4641-A.

Because of the rounding, estimate high. The registry counts every partial $500 as a whole one, so a price that lands just over a boundary costs the next full unit.

Who pays, the seller or the buyer?

Each side pays half. The grantor (seller) and grantee (buyer) split the tax under section 4641-A, and the register of deeds collects both shares when the deed is offered for recording.

That makes the seller's half a real line on the closing statement, and an easy one to overlook while comparing offers. If a buyer says they cover all closing costs, ask in writing whether that includes your half of the transfer tax.

When you disagree with the figure the register computes, section 4641-B allows a request that the State Tax Assessor determine the correct amount, so the deed can still be recorded.

What value is taxed?

The tax is figured on the value stated on the declaration, which is normally the price actually paid. Consideration usually means money, but it can also include other property or an assumed mortgage.

  • In an arm's-length sale, the value is the consideration.
  • For a gift, a nominal-price transfer or a deal where consideration cannot be determined, the value is fair market value.
  • Fair market value is presumed to equal the adjusted assessed value (the municipal assessed value divided by the municipality's certified ratio) unless the local assessor says otherwise.
  • "Nominal" means less than 20 percent of the adjusted assessed value.

Online preparers must enter the adjusted assessed value, which the municipal assessor can supply. This is why a $1 sale to a relative still gets taxed against what the town says the house is worth.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Maine house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Exempt sales and transfers

Maine exempts many deeds. For home sellers the common ones involve family, death, divorce, bankruptcy and certain lenders. Section 4641-C has the complete numbered list. The most relevant entries:

  • Deeds between spouses, parent and child, or grandparent and grandchild with no actual consideration, and deeds between spouses in divorce proceedings
  • Deeds of distribution under Title 18-B or Title 18-C, which covers an estate passing property to heirs
  • Transfers by transfer on death deed
  • Tax deeds and deeds given under the U.S. Bankruptcy Code
  • Corrective deeds that change nothing about price or ownership
  • Mortgage deeds, discharges and partial releases
  • Deeds to the U.S., the State or their agencies and subdivisions
  • Deeds to buyers receiving Maine State Housing Authority first-time homebuyer mortgage assistance, exempt for both buyer and seller
  • Conveyances of a mobile home park to a majority of its residents or a residents' association under Title 10, section 9094-A

An exemption never applies itself. It has to be claimed and named on the declaration, and section 4641-D requires the declaration to give the reason for any exempt transfer.

Foreclosure and deed in lieu

Distressed-sale deeds are taxed differently from ordinary sales. If you are behind on a mortgage, the differences are worth a look.

SituationWho owes tax
Deed in lieu of foreclosureThe mortgagor (owner) is exempt. The mortgagee pays half, based on the property's value.
Foreclosure auction sold to a third partyThe buyer pays half on the sale price. The seller pays half but only on any profit, so no profit means no seller tax.
Foreclosing lender is the high bidderThe lender is treated as both buyer and seller and pays the full tax on the sale price.
Mortgage deedNo tax for either party.

Handing a lender a deed in lieu costs the owner no transfer tax, while a regular sale before foreclosure carries the seller's half. Weigh that half against the other costs of each path.

Selling an LLC or other entity

The tax reaches entities too. Section 4641-A also taxes the transfer or acquisition of a controlling interest in an entity that holds Maine real estate, when it occurs within any 12-month period. The same rates apply to the property's value, and transferor and transferee each pay half.

A controlling-interest transfer is reported to the register of deeds and is not recorded as a deed. If the transfer goes unreported and the tax unpaid for 30 days after completion, both parties become jointly and severally liable for the entire amount. An owner who holds a rental in an LLC and plans to sell the company in place of the deed needs to know this. A transfer that would be exempt as a deed is exempt as a controlling-interest transfer too. Maine Revenue Services has a separate controlling interest declaration form.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Maine houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How and when it is collected

The register in the county where the property sits computes the tax and collects it at the moment the deed is offered for recording. No bill follows later. The declaration filed with the deed serves as the return, and the deed is not accepted until the money is in.

The register keeps 9.2 percent of the tax and sends 90.8 percent to Maine Revenue Services each month, and declarations reach the State within 40 days of recording. Under section 4641-B, registers remit by the 10th of each month for the prior month, with the State's share fixed at 90.8 percent for fiscal years 2025-26 and 2026-27.

For a seller the date that counts is closing day. The registry needs the declaration, the signed deed and payment all at once. Our Maine deed recording guide covers the fees and formatting that go with it.

Before closing, a seller's checklist

  1. Estimate the tax using the state's tax chart or estimate calculator, linked from the Maine Revenue Services transfer tax page.
  2. Ask who pays the seller's half and get the answer into the contract.
  3. Check whether your deed qualifies for an exemption and tell the closing agent so it goes on the declaration.
  4. If the buyer uses a Maine State Housing Authority first-time buyer loan, have the closer confirm the exemption for both sides.
  5. If the property sits inside an entity, ask a lawyer whether a controlling-interest transfer is involved.

This page is general information, not tax or legal advice. Maine Revenue Services answers calculation questions at prop.tax@maine.gov, and the county registry can confirm what it will accept on closing day.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Maine transfer tax rate?

$2.20 for each $500 or fraction of $500 of value. For transfers on or after November 1, 2025, value above $1 million adds $3.80 per $500, so that slice is taxed at $6.00 per $500.

Does the seller pay the transfer tax?

The seller pays half and the buyer pays half. Both shares are collected when the deed is recorded, so the seller's half normally comes out of proceeds at closing unless the contract says otherwise.

Is there transfer tax on an inherited house?

A deed of distribution from an estate under Title 18-B or 18-C is exempt. If the heirs then sell, that sale is taxed in the usual way and shared by seller and buyer.

Is a deed in lieu of foreclosure taxed?

The owner giving the deed is exempt. The lender pays half of the tax, based on the property's value.

Do first-time buyers pay the Maine transfer tax?

Buyers using a Maine State Housing Authority first-time homebuyer mortgage program are exempt, and so is the seller on that deed. The exemption has to be claimed on the declaration.

Where to record a deed

Take the deed to the registry of deeds for the county where the land lies. A parcel that crosses a county line must be recorded in every county it touches. Title 33, section 201 sets the rule, and where a county has more than one registry district, you use the district that is legal for that record.

Registries belong to the counties, not the state. Androscoggin County, for instance, runs its Registry of Deeds at 2 Turner Street, Unit 4, in Auburn, with an online search system. Knox County operates its own in Rockland and has used a 3:30 p.m. cutoff for same-day recording. Hours, mail-in rules and e-recording vendors vary, so phone the registry before you drive over or mail anything.

The town office is not where deeds go. The municipal assessor hears about a new owner later, when transfer information comes through the state. That lag is why tax records can trail the closing by a few weeks.

Recording fees

The base fee set by statute is $35 for a deed, and most registries add a $5 records preservation surcharge, so $40 is the usual bill. It is a flat charge per document. A ten-page deed costs what a two-page deed costs.

Document or serviceFee
Most instruments$35, plus the $5 surcharge a register may collect (total $40)
Instruments recorded at the request of the State or a municipality$25, with no surcharge
Plans$45 in statute, $50 per sheet on the registries' schedule
Paper copy$1 per page ($10 per page for plans)
Extra page added to fit the recording stamp$2 per added page

Payment is due when the document is offered for recording. Under the fee statute, the first 400 electronic images you pull from a county registry website in a calendar year are free, and each one after that costs 50 cents.

Transfer tax on a sale deed is a separate charge collected at the same counter. See our Maine transfer tax guide for the rates.

What a deed needs before the register accepts it

Bring the original signed deed with a named grantor and grantee, acknowledged before a notary or another authorized official. Registries also want a printed name under each signature and, for a company, the typed company name at the signature so it can be indexed.

Acknowledgment is a legal requirement, not a formality. Under section 203, most instruments must be acknowledged by the signer before a Maine notary, a Maine-admitted attorney or a listed out-of-state or foreign official. Court-issued instruments and certain foreclosure and tax lien documents follow different rules. Service members can acknowledge before designated commissioned officers.

Margins are where good deeds get bounced. The registers' margin standard, adopted May 20, 2024, asks for:

  • 3/4 inch on the sides of every page
  • 1 3/4 inches at the top of the first page and 1 inch at the top of later pages
  • 1 1/2 inches at the bottom of the last page
  • No punched holes, stickers or writing inside a margin

Section 653 lets a register charge $2 for each page added because the original left no room for recording information. A registry may also want blank space on the first page for its label. Knox County describes its label as 1 inch wide and 3 1/2 inches long.

The transfer tax declaration

Every sale deed travels with a Real Estate Transfer Tax Declaration. The register works out the tax from the value on it and collects before recording. The rate is $2.20 for each $500 of value, and buyer and seller split it. Under section 4641-B, proof of payment is an indicium attached to the declaration.

Section 4641-D spells out the contents: the value, the tax identification number of any business entity on either side, and the tax map and parcel number (or a statement that no suitable tax map exists). An exempt transfer has to name the exemption. Maine Revenue Services requires exemptions to be claimed on the form, because the register will not assume one.

A free state online database lets a preparer build the declaration, enter grantor and grantee identification numbers and send it to the registry. A rejected declaration triggers an email to the preparer. Deleting a rejected declaration is a mistake, because the registry cannot record the deed without it.

Within 40 days of recording, the register sends declarations to the State Tax Assessor, who forwards them to the municipal assessor by the 20th of the next month.

Deeds that skip the transfer tax but still get recorded

Several common seller situations avoid the tax and still need a recorded deed. The list in 36 M.R.S. section 4641-C includes the ones sellers meet most:

  • Deeds between spouses, parent and child, or grandparent and grandchild with no actual consideration
  • Deeds between spouses in divorce proceedings
  • Deeds of distribution from an estate under Title 18-C (and the older Title 18-B)
  • Transfers by transfer on death deed
  • Deeds given under the U.S. Bankruptcy Code
  • Corrective deeds that add no consideration and change no ownership
  • Deeds in lieu of foreclosure, where the owner giving the deed is exempt and the lender is not
  • Deeds to buyers using a Maine State Housing Authority first-time buyer mortgage program, exempt for both buyer and seller

A gift or nominal-price deed is taxed on fair market value unless an exemption applies, and the adjusted assessed value stands in for that value unless the local assessor says otherwise. A family transfer for real money is therefore not automatically exempt.

Why recording matters when you sell

A recorded, acknowledged deed protects the buyer against competing claims. Until it is recorded, the seller's name can remain on the public record. Section 201 makes a conveyance effective against third parties only once it is acknowledged and recorded, and a recorded deed beats an unrecorded one and unrecorded attachments.

Mortgage discharges are exempt from the tax and get recorded at the same registry. A paid-off loan whose discharge was never recorded can still appear on title when you sell. On a cash sale, the closing agent normally carries the deed, the declaration and the fees to the registry. Ask for the book and page number once it is done.

If your house has title wrinkles, such as an old unrecorded deed from a relative or a missing discharge, tell your buyer early. These are easier to clear before a closing date is set.

Mistakes that delay recording

  • The notary block is blank, or the signer's name differs from the typed name.
  • The first page has no room at the top for the recording stamp.
  • The declaration claims an exemption that does not fit the facts, or claims none when one applies.
  • The named seller has died and no distribution deed or personal representative's authority is attached.
  • A parcel in two counties is recorded in only one.
  • The check covers the old fee and leaves out the $5 surcharge.

Registries will usually quote the exact fee by phone, and Maine Revenue Services links declaration forms and a tax chart from its transfer tax page.

This guide is general information, not legal advice. A Maine attorney or title company can confirm what your particular deed requires.

Frequently asked questions

How much does it cost to record a deed in Maine?

The statute sets $35 per deed and most registries add a $5 surcharge, so $40 is typical. State and municipal filers pay $25, and transfer tax on a sale comes on top.

Do I record a deed with the county or the town?

With the county registry of deeds where the land sits. A parcel in two counties is recorded in both, and the town gets transfer information through the state afterward.

Does a Maine deed have to be notarized?

In nearly every case, yes. Section 203 requires most instruments to be acknowledged before a notary or other authorized official. Court-issued papers and certain foreclosure and tax lien documents follow other rules.

What margins does a Maine deed need?

The registers' standard asks for 3/4 inch on the sides, 1 3/4 inches at the top of page one, 1 inch at the top of later pages and 1 1/2 inches at the bottom of the last page. Stickers and holes are not allowed, and a register can charge $2 for each page it must add.

Can I record a deed myself?

Yes, since the registry is open to the public. The deed must be acknowledged and correctly formatted, with the declaration and fees. Many sellers leave it to the closing attorney or title company so a rejection does not delay the sale.
